Le groupe s’est de nouveau réuni le 5 se: The group gathered again on September 5 in front of the British Columbia legislature to demand changes to wellness checks and the creation of an Indigenous oversight body as part of the investigation into the death of Chantel Moore. It has been three months since the young woman was killed by a police officer during a wellness check in Edmundston, New Brunswick.
Depuis, sa famille et ses sympathisants: Since then, her family and supporters have continued to demand justice and changes to this police protocol. This is the second time since Chantel Moore’s death that her family and supporters have gathered on the steps of the British Columbia legislature. Once again, they demanded changes to wellness checks and the creation of an Indigenous oversight body.
« Nous sommes réunis ici aujourd’hui afi: “We are gathered here today to tell the country loudly that we will not sit idly by. No, we will no longer sit idly by,” said Marth Martin, Chantel’s mother. “I shouldn’t have to beg for justice for my daughter. Our children’s lives matter. My daughter was more than a number on a status card…”
Chantel Moore était membre de la Premièr: Chantel Moore was a member of the Tla-o-qui-aht First Nation. Her death is currently being investigated by the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI), the Quebec agency responsible for police oversight. Judith Sayers, president of the Nuu-chah-nulth Tribal Council, of which the Tla-o-qui-aht Nation is a member, was asked to speak on Ms. Martin’s behalf when she was overcome with emotion.
« Savez-vous quelle est l’ironie terribl: “Do you know what the terrible irony is in all of this?” Ms. Sayers continued. “The final report on missing and murdered Indigenous women was released exactly one year to the day before Chantel’s death. A measure that is supposed to change things in this country has, for all intents and purposes, not been implemented.”
On peut d’ailleurs lire dans le <l1>Rapp: The <l1>Final Report of the National Inquiry into Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls</l1> states that “[…] mistrust stemming from negative law enforcement experiences continues to foster an environment in which, as many participants pointed out, people don’t feel comfortable simply asking the police for help.”
<strong>Modifications aux contrôles de b: Changes to wellness checks and police work
Mme Sayers a ensuite ajouté que, dans le: Ms. Sayers then added that, under the circumstances, getting justice would mean getting changes to the way wellness checks are carried out across the country. In an interview with the <l1>Times Colonist</l1>, Ms. Martin said that Chantel’s boyfriend, who lives in Toronto, had asked the police to do a wellness check on the young woman because he feared she was being harassed.
Selon Del Manak, chef de la police de Vi: According to Del Manak, Victoria’s police chief, who was at the rally on the steps of the legislature, a police officer carries out a wellness check when they are called and asked to go see how a person is doing because there are concerns for their well-being. He also said in an interview that people who make this type of call do so “for a multitude of reasons,” which are often related to mental health issues.
« Ce qu’on demande, c’est que Chantel ob: “What we’re asking for is justice for Chantel and a complete rethink of wellness checks,” Ms. Sayers summed up. “Responders who understand the trauma people are dealing with, not police officers, should be the first to respond during these checks.”
Le Rapport final <l1>recommande</l1> aus: The Final Report also <l1>recommends</l1> that mental health services be integrated into various sectors, including the criminal justice system, housing services and child and family protection services. It states that “[when it comes to trauma-informed services, a sense of safety is created in every interaction” and that “[adopting a trauma-informed approach across all policies, procedures and practices related to solutions and services is essential to implementing the Calls for Justice.”

Jeremy Son, le policier qui a abattu la: Jeremy Son, the police officer who shot and killed the young Indigenous woman, was first placed on paid leave but was later reinstated and assigned to administrative duties. Ms. Moore’s family filed <l1>two complaints</l1> against Edmundston police officers with the New Brunswick Police Commission. One calls for Officer Son’s dismissal. The other is a complaint against an officer who laughed while talking about the tragedy in a video interview with CTV News on June 5. The Tla-o-qui-aht hereditary chiefs issued <l2>a statement</l2> on June 20 calling for Officer Jeremy Son to be charged with murder under the Criminal Code of Canada. They said Ms. Moore’s death “seems senseless, preventable and like an act of systemic racism” to them.
La famille de Mme Moore s’est aussi dite: Ms. Moore’s family has also expressed concern that the <l1>BEI</l1> may not recommend charges against the officer who shot and killed the young woman. In the 125 independent investigations the Bureau has opened following cases of injury or death caused by police officers, no charges have been laid against police. At the September 5 rally, Ms. Sayers also said she hoped Indigenous people would take part in handling complaints against the police.
« De cette manière, il y aurait une comp: “That way, there would be an understanding of Indigenous ways of doing things, Indigenous knowledge,” she explained. “We need an Indigenous oversight body for all police forces in Canada.”
Les députés néo-démocrates Gord Johns (C: NDP MPs Gord Johns (Courtenay–Alberni) and Laurel Collins (Victoria) also took part in the rally. Mr. Johns’s riding covers part of Nuu-chah-nulth territory. Ms. Sayers noted that the MP offered his support to Ms. Moore’s family “from the very beginning.”
Johns et Mme Collins, qui se sont tous d: Johns and Ms. Collins, who both said they support changes to wellness checks across the country, pledged that they would keep calling for such changes.
« Nous devons faire en sorte que les cit: “We have to make sure that citizens, particularly Indigenous people, have confidence in a police oversight process,” Ms. Collins said in an interview. “We also have to make sure we change the way police officers do their work and the way wellness checks are carried out. All of these things are part of the systemic racism that is rampant in most of our communities.”
